entries.c638575878f13a99b1e9d9cf984a155eb191b65e: <div sID="gen21125" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="Mal.4" sID="Mal.4"/> <div eID="gen21125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21126" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21127" type="x-p"/> We have here proper instructions given us (very proper to close the canon of the Old Testament with), I. Concerning the state of recompence and retribution that is before us, the misery of the wicked and the happiness of the righteous in that state, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1-Mal.4.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. And this is represented to us under a prophecy of the destruction of Jerusalem, and the unbelieving Jews with it, and of the comforts and triumphs of those among them that received the gospel. II. Concerning the state of trial and preparation we are now in, in which we are directed to have an eye to divine revelation, and to follow that; they then must keep to the law of Moses (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.4">ver. 4</reference>) and expect a further discovery of God's will by Elijah the prophet, that is, by John Baptist, the harbinger of the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.5-Mal.4.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. The last chapter of the New Testament is much to the same purport, setting before us heaven and hell in the other world, and obliging us to adhere to the word of God in this world.
entries.d78417fecb0b9cbc442ddf52ac1019c8661782f0: <div eID="gen21127" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21126" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Predictions. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 400.)</title> <div sID="gen21128" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch. <hi type="super">2</hi> But unto you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise with healing in his wings; and ye shall go forth, and grow up as calves of the stall. <hi type="super">3</hi> And ye shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I shall do <hi type="italic">this,</hi> saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts. <div eID="gen21128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21129" type="x-p"/> The great and terrible day of the Lord is here prophesied of. This, like the pillar of cloud and fire, shall have a dark side turned towards the Egyptians that fight against God, and a bright side towards the faithful Israelites that follow him: <hi type="italic">The day cometh,</hi> that is, the Lord cometh, the day of the Lord; and it has reference both to the first and to the second coming of Jesus Christ; the day of both was fixed, and should answer the character here given of it. <div eID="gen21129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21130" type="x-p"/> I. In both Christ is a consuming fire to those that rebel against him. The day of his coming <hi type="italic">shall burn as an oven;</hi> it shall be a day of wrath, of <hi type="italic">fiery indignation.</hi> This was foretold concerning the Messiah, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Ps. xxi. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thy hand shall find out all thy enemies,</hi> and <hi type="italic">shall make them as a fiery oven in the time of thy anger.</hi> It will be a day of terror and destruction like the burning of a city, or rather of a wood, the trees whereof are withered and dried, for to that the allusion seems to be, as <reference osisRef="Isa.10.17-Isa.10.18">Isa. x. 17, 18</reference>, <hi type="italic">The light of Israel shall be for a fire, and his Holy One for a flame, and it shall consume the glory of his forest and of his fruitful field.</hi> Now observe here, 1. Who shall be fuel to this fire—all <hi type="italic">the proud</hi> in heart, whose words have been stout against God, and their necks stiff and unapt to yield to the yoke of his commandments (all those that <hi type="italic">in the pride of their countenances will not seek after God,</hi> nor submit to the grace and government of Jesus Christ—all that proudly say they <hi type="italic">will not have Christ to reign over them</hi>), and all those that <hi type="italic">do wickedly</hi> in their affections and conversations, that wilfully persist in sin, in contempt of and contradiction to the law of God; they are such as <hi type="italic">do wickedly against the covenant,</hi> as another prophet had lately expressed it, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.32">Dan. xi. 32</reference>. God, that has perfect knowledge of every one's character, knows who are <hi type="italic">the proud,</hi> and of every one's actions, knows who they are that <hi type="italic">do wickedly;</hi> and they shall be as <hi type="italic">stubble</hi> to this fire; they shall be consumed by it, easily consumed, utterly consumed, and it is wholly owing to themselves that they shall be so, for they make themselves stubble, that is, combustible matter, to this fire. If they were not stubble, it would not burn them; for the fire will be to every man according as he and his works are found; if they be <hi type="italic">wood, hay,</hi> and <hi type="italic">stubble,</hi> they will be <hi type="italic">consumed;</hi> but if they be <hi type="italic">gold, silver, and precious stones,</hi> they will <hi type="italic">abide the fire</hi> and be purified by it, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.13-1Cor.3.15">1 Cor. iii. 13-15</reference>. Those that by their unbelief oppose Christ thereby set themselves as <hi type="italic">briers and thorns</hi> before a <hi type="italic">devouring fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.27.4-Isa.27.5">Isa. xxvii. 4, 5</reference>. 2. What shall be the force and what the fruit of this fire: <hi type="italic">The day that cometh shall burn them up,</hi> shall both terrify and ruin them, and shall <hi type="italic">leave them neither root nor branch,</hi> neither <hi type="italic">son</hi> nor <hi type="italic">nephew</hi> (so the Chaldee paraphrase): neither they nor their posterity shall be spared; they shall be wholly extirpated and cut off. <hi type="italic">Who knows the power of God's anger? The proud and those that do wickedly</hi> will not fear it, but they shall be made to feel it. Where are those now that <hi type="italic">called the proud happy,</hi> when thus they are made completely miserable, when there remains no branch of their happiness to be enjoyed for the present, nor any root of it out of which it might again spring up? Now this was fulfilled, (1.) When Christ, in his doctrine, spoke terror and condemnation to the proud Pharisees and the other Jews that did wickedly, when he sent that fire on the earth which burnt up the chaff of the traditions of the elders and the corrupt glosses they had put upon the law of God. (2.) When Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, and the nation of the Jews, as a nation, quite blotted out from under heaven, and neither root nor branch left them. This seems to be principally intended here; our Saviour says that those should be the <hi type="italic">days of vengeance,</hi> when all the things that were written to that purport should be fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Luke.21.22">Luke xxi. 22</reference>. Then the unbelieving Jews were as stubble to the devouring fire of God's judgments, which gathered together to them as the eagles to the carcase. (3.) It is certainly applicable, and is to be applied, to the day of judgment, to the particular judgment at death (some of the Jewish doctors refer it the <hi type="italic">punishment that seizes on the souls of the wicked immediately after they go out of the body</hi>), but especially to the general judgment, at the end of time, when Christ shall be <hi type="italic">revealed in flaming fire,</hi> to execute judgment on <hi type="italic">the proud, and all that do wickedly.</hi> The whole world shall then <hi type="italic">burn as an oven,</hi> and all the children of this world, that set their hearts upon it and choose their portion in it, shall take their ruin with it, and the fire then kindled shall never be quenched. <div eID="gen21130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21131" type="x-p"/> II. In both Christ is a rejoicing light to those who serve him faithfully, to those who fear his name and give him the glory due to it (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">v. 2</reference>), who stand in awe of that name of his which the wicked profane and trample upon. Here are mercy and comfort kept in store for all those who fear the Lord and think on his name. Observe, <div eID="gen21131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21132" type="x-p"/> 1. Whence this mercy and comfort shall flow to them: <hi type="italic">To you that fear my name shall the Sun of righteousness arise, with healing in his wings.</hi> The day that comes, as it will be a stormy day to the wicked, a day in which God will rain upon them <hi type="italic">fire and brimstone, and a horrible tempest,</hi> as he did on Sodom (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Ps. xi. 6</reference>), a <hi type="italic">day of clouds and thick darkness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.5.18">Amos v. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.20">20</reference>), so it will be a fair and bright day to those who fear God, and reviving as the rising sun is to the earth; and particular notice is taken of the rising of the sun upon Zoar when that was mercifully distinguished from the cities of the plain, which the fire <hi type="italic">consumed;</hi> see <reference osisRef="Gen.19.23">Gen. xix. 23</reference>. So to those that fear God is comfort spoken. When the hearts of others <hi type="italic">fail for fear</hi> let them <hi type="italic">lift up their heads for joy,</hi> for <hi type="italic">their redemption draws nigh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.21.28">Luke xxi. 28</reference>. But by the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> here we are certainly to understand Jesus Christ, who would undertake to secure the believing remnant, in the day of the general destruction of the Jews, from falling with the rest, and to comfort them in that day of distress and perplexity with his consolations; he directed those that were in Judea to <hi type="italic">flee to the mountains</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.16">Matt. xxiv. 16</reference>), and they did so, and were all safe and easy in Pella. But it is to be applied more generally, (1.) To the coming of Christ in the flesh to seek and save those that were lost; then the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness</hi> arose upon this dark world. Christ is the <hi type="italic">light of the world,</hi> the true light, the great light that makes day and rules the day (<reference osisRef="John.8.12">John viii. 12</reference>), as the sun. He is the <hi type="italic">light of men</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.1.4">John i. 4</reference>), is to men's souls as the sun is to the visible world, which without the sun would be a dungeon; so would mankind be darkness itself without the <hi type="italic">light of the glory of God</hi> shining <hi type="italic">in the face of Christ.</hi> Christ is the Sun that has light in himself, and is the fountain of light (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.4-Ps.19.6">Ps. xix. 4-6</reference>); he is the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness,</hi> for he is himself a righteous Saviour. Righteousness is both the light and the heat of this Sun; the word of his righteousness is so; it guides, instructs, and quickens; so is the <hi type="italic">everlasting righteousness</hi> he has brought in. He is <hi type="italic">made of God to us righteousness;</hi> he is the <hi type="italic">Lord our righteousness,</hi> and therefore is fitly called <hi type="italic">the Sun of righteousness.</hi> Through him we are justified and sanctified, and so are brought to see light. This Sun of righteousness, in the fulness of time, arose upon the world, and with him <hi type="italic">light came into the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.3.19">John iii. 19</reference>), a <hi type="italic">great light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.4.16">Matt. iv. 16</reference>. In him <hi type="italic">the day-spring from on high visited us, to give light to those that sit in darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.1.78-Luke.1.79">Luke i. 78, 79</reference>. Righteousness sometimes signifies mercy or benignity, and it was in Christ that the <hi type="italic">tender mercy of our God</hi> visited us. (2.) It is applicable to the graces and comforts of the Holy Spirit, brought into the souls of men. Grotius understands it of Christ's giving the Spirit to those that are his, to shine in their hearts, and to be a <hi type="italic">comforter</hi> to them, a <hi type="italic">sun and a shield.</hi> Those that are possessed and governed by a holy fear of God and a dread of his majesty shall have his <hi type="italic">love</hi> also <hi type="italic">shed abroad in their hearts by the Holy Ghost;</hi> and then the sun may be said to arise there, and to bring both a delightful day and a fruitful spring along with it. (3.) Christ's second coming will be a glorious and welcome sun-rising to all that <hi type="italic">fear his name;</hi> it will be that morning of the resurrection in which <hi type="italic">the upright shall have dominion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Ps. xlix. 14</reference>. That day which to the wicked will <hi type="italic">burn as an oven</hi> will to the righteous be bright as the morning; and it is what they wait for, <hi type="italic">more than those that wait for the morning.</hi> <div eID="gen21132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21133" type="x-p"/> 2. What this mercy and comfort shall bring to them: He <hi type="italic">shall arise with healing under his wings,</hi> or in his <hi type="italic">rays</hi> or <hi type="italic">beams,</hi> which are as the wings of the sun. Christ came, as <hi type="italic">the sun,</hi> to bring not only light to a dark world, but health to a diseased distempered world. The Jews (says Dr. Pocock) have a proverbial saying, <hi type="italic">As the sun riseth, infirmities decrease;</hi> the flowers which drooped and languished all night revive in the morning. Christ came into the world to be the great physician, yea, and the great medicine too, both the balm in Gilead and the physician there. When he was upon earth, he went about as the sun in his circuit, doing this good; he <hi type="italic">healed all manner of sicknesses and diseases among the people;</hi> he healed by wholesale, as the sun does. He shall arise <hi type="italic">with healing in his skirts;</hi> so some read it, and they apply it to the story of the woman's touching <hi type="italic">the hem of his garment,</hi> and being thereby <hi type="italic">made whole,</hi> and his finding that <hi type="italic">virtue went out of him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.5.28-Mark.5.30">Mark v. 28-30</reference>. But his healing bodily diseases was a specimen of his great design in coming into the world to heal the diseases of men's souls, and to put them into a good state of health, that they may serve and enjoy both God and themselves. <div eID="gen21133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21134" type="x-p"/> 3. What good effect it shall have upon them. (1.) It shall make them vigorous in themselves: "<hi type="italic">You shall go forth,</hi> as those that are healed go abroad and return to their business." The souls shall go forth out of their bodies at death, and the bodies out of their graves at the resurrection, as prisoners out of their dungeons, and both to see the light and be set at liberty. "<hi type="italic">You shall go forth</hi> as plants out of the earth, when in the spring the sun returns." Some make it to mean the going forth of the Christians from Jerusalem, and the escape they thereby made from its destruction. And thus the souls on whom the Sun of righteousness arises go forth out of the world, go forth out of Babylon, as those that are made <hi type="italic">free indeed.</hi> "You shall likewise <hi type="italic">grow up;</hi> being restored to health and liberty, you shall increase in knowledge, and grace, and spiritual strength." The souls on which the Sun of righteousness arises are growing up towards <hi type="italic">the perfect man;</hi> those that by the grace of God are made wise and good are by the same grace made wiser and better; and their path, like that of the rising sun, <hi type="italic">shines more and more to the perfect day,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.4.18">Prov. iv. 18</reference>. Their growth is compared to that of <hi type="italic">the calves of the stall,</hi> which is a quick, strong, and useful growth. "You shall grow up, not as the <hi type="italic">flower of the field,</hi> which is slender, and weak, and of little use, and withers soon after it has grown up, but as the <hi type="italic">calves of the stall,</hi>" that, as one of the rabbin expounds it, <hi type="italic">grow great in flesh and fatness,</hi> with which both God's altars and men's tables are replenished; so the growth of the saints, on whom the Sun of righteousness arises, honours both God and man. Some read it, instead of <hi type="italic">You shall grow up,</hi> You shall <hi type="italic">move yourselves,</hi> or <hi type="italic">leap for joy,</hi> shall be as frolicsome as calves of the stall, when they are let loose in the open field; it denotes the joy of the saints, who rejoice in Christ Jesus; they shall even leap for joy; they are <hi type="italic">always caused to triumph.</hi> <div eID="gen21134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21135" type="x-p"/> (2.) It shall make them victorious over their enemies (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">You shall tread down the wicked.</hi> Time was when the wicked trod them down, said to their souls, <hi type="italic">Bow down, that we may go over;</hi> but the day will come when they shall <hi type="italic">tread down the wicked.</hi> The wicked, being made Christ's footstool, are made theirs also (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">Ps. cx. 1</reference>), and come and <hi type="italic">worship before the feet</hi> of the church, <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. <hi type="italic">The elder shall serve the younger.</hi> When believers by faith <hi type="italic">overcome the world,</hi> when they suppress their own corrupt appetites and passions, when the God of peace bruises Satan under their feet, then they <hi type="italic">tread down the wicked.</hi> When it came to the turn of the Christians to triumph over the Jews that had insulted over them, then this promise was fulfilled: <hi type="italic">They shall be ashes under the soles of your feet;</hi> they shall not only be <hi type="italic">trodden down,</hi> but trodden <hi type="italic">to dirt.</hi> When the day that comes shall have <hi type="italic">burnt them up,</hi> they shall trample upon them as ashes. When the righteous shall rise to <hi type="italic">everlasting life,</hi> the wicked shall rise to <hi type="italic">everlasting contempt;</hi> and, though they shall not triumph over them, they shall triumph in that God whose justice is glorified in their destruction. The saints in glory are said to have power given them over the nations, to <hi type="italic">rule them with a rod of iron,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26-Rev.2.27">Rev. ii. 26, 27</reference>. This <hi type="italic">you shall do, in the day that I shall do this.</hi> Note, The saints' triumphs are all owing to God's victories; it is not they that do this, but God that does it for them, that says, <hi type="italic">Come set your feet on the necks of these kings.</hi> Some read it, "<hi type="italic">In the day that I make,</hi> or shall make, the <hi type="italic">great day</hi> that I shall make remarkable, of which you will say with joy, <hi type="italic">This is the day which the Lord has made.</hi>" The day of the destruction of Jerusalem is called the <hi type="italic">great and notable day of the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.20">Acts ii. 20</reference>), and our Saviour in foretelling that destruction made use of such expressions as, like these, might be applied likewise to the <hi type="italic">end of the world</hi> and the <hi type="italic">last judgment;</hi> for it was such a terrible revelation of the wrath of God from heaven, and caused such a scene of horror upon this earth, that it might fitly serve for a type of that glorious transaction which will be an outlet to the days of time and an inlet to the days of eternity. By the accomplishment of these prophecies in the ruin of the Jewish nation, we should have our faith confirmed in the assurances Christ has given us concerning the dissolution of all things. <hi type="italic">Surely I come quickly;</hi> so says Christ, <hi type="italic">the Lord of hosts,</hi> to whom all power in heaven and earth is committed.
entries.c9bc8558daeb02f1a572ade587bcfb9915dd8b56: <div eID="gen21135" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Evangelical Predictions. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 400.)</title> <div sID="gen21136" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Remember ye the law of Moses my servant, which I commanded unto him in Horeb for all Israel, <hi type="italic">with</hi> the statutes and judgments. <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : <hi type="super">6</hi> And he shall turn the heart of the fathers to the children, and the heart of the children to their fathers, lest I come and smite the earth with a curse. <div eID="gen21136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21137" type="x-p"/> This is doubtless intended for a solemn conclusion, not only of this prophecy, but of the canon of the Old Testament, and is a plain information that they were not to expect any more sayings nor writing by divine inspiration, any more of the dictates of the Spirit of prophecy, till the beginning of the gospel of the Messiah, which sets aside the Apocrypha as no part of holy writ, and which therefore the Jews never received. <div eID="gen21137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21138" type="x-p"/> Now that prophecy ceases, and is about to be sealed up, there are two things required of the people of God, that lived then:— <div eID="gen21138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21139" type="x-p"/> I. They must keep up an obedient veneration for the law of Moses (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Remember the law of Moses my servant,</hi> and observe to do according to it, even that law which <hi type="italic">I commanded unto him in Horeb,</hi> that fiery law which was intended <hi type="italic">for all Israel, with the statutes and judgments,</hi> not only the law of the ten commandments, but all the other appointments, ceremonial and judicial, then and there given. Observe here, 1. The honourable mention that is made of <hi type="italic">Moses,</hi> the first writer of the Old Testament, in <hi type="italic">Malachi,</hi> the last writer. God by him calls him <hi type="italic">Moses my servant;</hi> for the righteous shall be had in everlasting remembrance. See how the penmen of scripture, though they lived in several ages at a great distance from each other (it was above 1200 years from Moses to Malachi), all concurred in the same thing, and supported one another, being all actuated and guided by one and the same Spirit. 2. The honourable mention that is made of the <hi type="italic">law of Moses;</hi> it was what God himself <hi type="italic">commanded;</hi> he owns it for his law, and he commanded it <hi type="italic">for all Israel,</hi> as the municipal law of their kingdom. Thus will God <hi type="italic">magnify his law and make it honourable.</hi> Note, We are concerned to keep the law because God has commanded it and commanded it for us, for we are the spiritual Israel; and, if we expect the benefit of the covenant with Israel (<reference osisRef="Heb.8.10">Heb. viii. 10</reference>), we must observe the commands given to Israel, those of them that were intended to be of perpetual obligation. 3. The summary of our duty, with reference to the law. We must remember it. Forgetfulness of the law is at the bottom of all our transgressions of it; if we would rightly remember it, we could not but conform to it. We should remember it when we have occasion to use it, remember both the commands themselves and the sanctions wherewith they are enforced. The office of conscience is to bid us <hi type="italic">remember the law.</hi> But how does this charge to remember the law of Moses come in here? (1.) This prophet had reproved them for many gross corruptions and irregularities both in worship and conversation, and now, for the reforming and amending of what was amiss, he only charges them to <hi type="italic">remember the law of Moses:</hi> "Keep to that rule, and you will do all you should do." He will <hi type="italic">lay upon them no other burden</hi> than what they <hi type="italic">have received; hold that fast,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.2.24-Rev.2.25">Rev. ii. 24, 25</reference>. Note, Corrupt churches are to be reformed by the written word, and reduced into order by being reduced to the standard of <hi type="italic">the law and the testimony,</hi> see <reference osisRef="1Cor.11.23">1 Cor. xi. 23</reference>. (2.) The church had long enjoyed the benefit of prophets, extraordinary messengers from God, and now they had a whole book of their prophecies put together, and it was a finished piece; but they must not think that hereby the <hi type="italic">law of Moses</hi> was superseded, and had become as an almanac out of date, as if now they were advanced to a higher form and might forget that. No; the prophets do but confirm and apply the law, and press the observance of that; and therefore still <hi type="italic">Remember the law.</hi> Note, Even when we have made considerable advances in knowledge we must still retain the first principles of practical religion and resolve to abide by them. Those that study the writings of the prophets, and the apocalypse, must still remember the law of Moses and the four gospels. (3.) Prophecy was now to cease in the church for some ages, and the Spirit of prophecy not to return till the <hi type="italic">beginning of the gospel,</hi> and now they are told to <hi type="italic">remember the law of Moses;</hi> let them live by the rules of that, and live upon the promises of that. Note, We need not complain for want of visions and revelations as long as we have the written word, and the canon of scripture complete, to be our guide; for that is the most <hi type="italic">sure word of prophecy,</hi> and the touchstone by which we are to <hi type="italic">try the spirits.</hi> Though we have not prophets, yet, as long as we have Bibles, we may keep our communion with God, and keep ourselves in his way. (4.) They were to expect the coming of the Messiah, the preaching of his gospel, and the setting up of his kingdom, and in that expectation they must <hi type="italic">remember the law of Moses,</hi> and live in obedience to that, and then they might expect the comforts that the Messiah would bring to <hi type="italic">the willing and obedient.</hi> Let them observe the law of Moses, and live up to the light which that gave them, and then they might expect the benefit of the gospel of Christ, for <hi type="italic">to him that has,</hi> and uses what he has well, <hi type="italic">more shall be given, and he shall have abundance.</hi> <div eID="gen21139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21140" type="x-p"/> II. They must keep up a believing expectation of the gospel of Christ, and must look for the beginning of it in the appearing of Elijah the prophet (<reference osisRef="Mal.4.5-Mal.4.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet.</hi> Though the Spirit of prophecy cease for a time, and you will have only the law to consult, yet it shall revive again in one that shall be sent <hi type="italic">in the spirit and power of Elias,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Luke i. 17</reference>. The <hi type="italic">law and the prophets were until John</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Luke xvi. 16</reference>); they continued to be the only lights of the church till that morning-star appeared. Note, As God never <hi type="italic">left himself without witness</hi> in the world, so neither in the church, but, as there was occasion, carried the light of divine revelation further and further to the perfect day. They had now Moses and the prophets, and might hear them; but God will go further: he will send them Elijah. Observe, <div eID="gen21140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21141" type="x-p"/> 1. Who this prophet is that shall be sent; it is <hi type="italic">Elijah.</hi> The Jewish doctors will have it to be the same Elijah that prophesied in Israel in the days of Ahab—that he shall come again to be the forerunner of the Messiah; yet others of them say not the same person, but another of the same spirit. It should seem, those different sentiments they had when they asked John, "<hi type="italic">Art thou Elias,</hi> or <hi type="italic">that prophet</hi> that should bear his name?" <reference osisRef="John.1.19-John.1.21">John i. 19-21</reference>. But we Christians know very well that John Baptist was the Elias that was to come, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.10-Matt.17.13">Matt. xvii. 10-13</reference>; and very expressly, <reference osisRef="Matt.11.14">Matt. xi. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">This is Elias that was to come;</hi> and <reference osisRef="Mal.4.10">v. 10</reference>, the same of whom it is written, <hi type="italic">Behold, I send my messenger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">ch. iii. 1</reference>. Elijah was a man of great austerity and mortification, zealous for God, bold in reproving sin, and active to reduce an apostate people to God and their duty; John Baptist was animated by the same spirit and power, and preached repentance and reformation, as Elias had done; and all held him for a prophet, as they did Elijah in his day, and that his baptism was <hi type="italic">from heaven,</hi> and not <hi type="italic">of men.</hi> Note, When God has such work to do as was formerly to be done he can raise up such men to do it as he formerly raised up, and can put into a John Baptist the spirit of an Elias. <div eID="gen21141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21142" type="x-p"/> 2. When he shall be sent—before the appearing of the Messiah, which, because it was the judgment of this world, and introduced the ruin of the Jewish church and nation, is here called the <hi type="italic">coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord.</hi> John Baptist gave them fair warning of this when he told them of the <hi type="italic">wrath to come</hi> (that <hi type="italic">wrath to the uttermost</hi> which was hastening upon them) and put them into a way of escape from it, and when he told them of the <hi type="italic">fan in Christ's hand,</hi> with which Christ would thoroughly purge his floor; see <reference osisRef="Matt.3.7">Matt. iii. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.10">10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">12</reference>. That day of Christ, when he came first, was as that day will be when he comes again—though a great and joyful day to those that embrace him, yet a <hi type="italic">great and dreadful day</hi> to those that oppose him. John Baptist was sent before the coming of this day, to give people notice of it, that they might get ready for it, and go forth to meet it. <div eID="gen21142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21143" type="x-p"/> 3. On what errand he shall be sent: <hi type="italic">He shall turn the heart of the fathers to their children, and the heart of the children to their fathers;</hi> that is, "he shall be employed in this work; he shall attempt it; his doctrine and baptism shall have a direct tendency to it, and with many shall be successful: he shall be an instrument in God's hand of <hi type="italic">turning</hi> many <hi type="italic">to righteousness,</hi> to <hi type="italic">the Lord their God,</hi> and so <hi type="italic">making ready a people prepared for him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Luke.1.16-Luke.1.17">Luke i. 16, 17</reference>. Note, The turning of souls to God and their duty is the best preparation of them for the great and dreadful day of the Lord. It is promised concerning John, (1.) That he shall give a turn to things, shall make a bold stand against the strong torrent of sin and impiety which he found in full force among the children of his people, and beating down all before it. This is called his <hi type="italic">coming to restore all things</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">Matt. xvii. 11</reference>), to set them to rights, that they may again go in the right channel. (2.) That he shall preach a doctrine that shall reach men's hearts, and have an influence upon them, and work a change in them. God's word, in his mouth, shall be <hi type="italic">quick</hi> and <hi type="italic">powerful,</hi> and a <hi type="italic">discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.</hi> Many had their consciences awakened by his ministry who yet were not thoroughly wrought upon, such a spirit and power was there in it. (3.) That he shall turn the hearts of the fathers with the children, and of the children with the fathers (for so some read it), to God and to their duty. He shall call upon young and old to repent, and shall not labour in vain, for many of the fathers that are going off, and many of the children that are growing up, shall be wrought upon by his ministry. (4.) That thus he shall be an instrument to revive and confirm love and unity among relations, and shall bring them closer and bind them faster to each other, by bringing and binding them all to their God. He shall prepare the way for that kingdom of heaven which will make all its faithful subjects of <hi type="italic">one heart</hi> and <hi type="italic">one soul</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.4.32">Acts iv. 32</reference>), which will be a kingdom of love, and will slay all enmities. <div eID="gen21143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21144" type="x-p"/> 4. With what view he shall be sent on this errand: <hi type="italic">Lest I come and smite the earth,</hi> that is, the land of Israel, the body of the Jewish nation (that were of the earth earthy), <hi type="italic">with a curse.</hi> They by their impiety and impenitence in it had laid themselves open to the curse of God, which is a separation to all evil. God was ready to smite them with that curse, to bring utter ruin upon them, to strike home, to strike dead, with the curse; but he will yet once more try them, whether they will repent and return, and so prevent it; and therefore he sends John Baptist to preach repentance to them, that their conversion might prevent their confusion; so unwilling is God that any should perish, so willing to have his anger turned away. Had they universally repented and reformed, their repentance would have had this desired effect; but, they generally rejecting the counsel of God in John's baptism, it proved against themselves (<reference osisRef="Luke.7.30">Luke vii. 30</reference>) and their land was smitten with the curse which both it and they lie under to this day. Note, Those must expect to be smitten with a sword, with a curse, who <hi type="italic">turn not to him that smites them</hi> with a rod, with a cross, <reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Isa. ix. 13</reference>. Now the <hi type="italic">axe is laid to the root of the tree,</hi> says John Baptist, and it is ready to be smitten, to be cut down, <hi type="italic">with a curse;</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">bring forth fruit meet for repentance.</hi> Some observe that the last word of the Old Testament is a curse, which threatens the earth (<reference osisRef="Zech.5.3">Zech. v. 3</reference>), our desert of which we must be made sensible of, that we may bid Christ welcome, who comes with a blessing; and it is with a blessing, with the choicest of blessings, that the New Testament ends, and with it let us arm ourselves, or rather let God arm us, against this curse. <hi type="italic">The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with us all. Amen.</hi> <<<< <div eID="gen21144" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mal.4"/> <title type="x-s2">PREFACE</title> <div canonical="true" eID="gen21038" osisID="Mal" type="book"/>

entries.05e41f3bcb38a7e88130da25511fc8ff2c96845a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13263"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <title type="x-s3">Mal 4:1-6. God's Coming Judgment: Triumph of the Godly: Return to the law THE Best Preparation for Jehovah's Coming: Elijah's Preparatory Mission of Reformation.</title> <div sID="gen25091" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13263"/><hi type="bold">1. the day cometh ... burn--</hi>(Mal 3:2; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.7">2Pe 3:7</reference>). Primarily is meant the judgment coming on Jerusalem; but as this will not exhaust the meaning, without supposing what is inadmissible in Scripture--exaggeration--the final and full accomplishment, of which the former was the earnest, is the day of general judgment. This principle of interpretation is not double, but successive fulfilment. The language is abrupt, "Behold, the day cometh! It burns like a furnace." The abruptness imparts terrible reality to the picture, as if it suddenly burst on the prophet's view.<div eID="gen25091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25092" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the proud--</hi>in opposition to the cavil above (Mal 3:15), "now we call the proud (haughty despisers of God) happy."<div eID="gen25092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25093" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stubble--</hi>(Ob 18; <reference osisRef="Matt.3.12">Mt 3:12</reference>). As Canaan, the inheritance of the Israelites, was prepared for their possession by purging out the heathen, so judgment on the apostates shall usher in the entrance of the saints upon the Lord's inheritance, of which Canaan is the type--not heaven, but earth to its utmost bounds (<reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Psa 2:8</reference>) purged of all things that offend (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.41">Mt 13:41</reference>), which are to be "gathered out of His kingdom," the scene of the judgment being that also of the kingdom. The present dispensation is a spiritual kingdom, parenthetical between the Jews' literal kingdom and its antitype, the coming literal kingdom of the Lord Jesus.<div eID="gen25093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25094" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">neither root nor branch--</hi>proverbial for utter destruction (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Am 2:9</reference>). <div eID="gen25094" type="x-p"/>
entries.e36423a9218f08edb2fe9c75827353311f970557: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13264"/><div sID="gen25095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13264"/>2. The effect of the judgment on the righteous, as contrasted with its effect on the wicked (Mal 4:1). To the wicked it shall be as an oven that consumes the stubble (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.30">Mt 6:30</reference>); to the righteous it shall be the advent of the gladdening Sun, not of condemnation, but "of righteousness"; not destroying, but "healing" (<reference osisRef="Jer.23.6">Jr 23:6</reference>).<div eID="gen25095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25096" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">you that fear my name--</hi>The same as those in Mal 3:16, who confessed God amidst abounding blasphemy (<reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">Is 66:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.32">Mt 10:32</reference>). The spiritual blessings brought by Him are summed up in the two, "righteousness" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.1.30">1Co 1:30</reference>) and spiritual "healing" (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.57.19">Is 57:19</reference>). Those who walk in the dark now may take comfort in the certainty that they shall walk hereafter in eternal light (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Is 50:10</reference>).<div eID="gen25096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25097" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in his wings--</hi>implying the winged swiftness with which He shall appear (compare "suddenly," Mal 3:1) for the relief of His people. The beams of the Sun are His "wings." Compare "wings of the morning," <reference osisRef="Ps.139.9">Psa 139:9</reference>. The "Sun" gladdening the righteous is suggested by the previous "day" of terror consuming the wicked. Compare as to Christ, <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2Sa 23:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Psa 84:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.1.78">Lu 1:78</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.1.9">Joh 1:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.12">8:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.14">Ep 5:14</reference>; and in His second coming, <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2Pe 1:19</reference>. The Church is the moon reflecting His light (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.1">Re 12:1</reference>). The righteous shall by His righteousness "shine as the Sun in the kingdom of the Father" (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.43">Mt 13:43</reference>).<div eID="gen25097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25098" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye shall go forth--</hi>from the straits in which you were, as it were, held captive. An earnest of this was given in the escape of the Christians to Pella before the destruction of Jerusalem.<div eID="gen25098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25099" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grow up--</hi>rather, "leap" as frisking calves [Calvin]; literally, "spread," "take a wide range."<div eID="gen25099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as calves of the stall--</hi>which when set free from the stall disport with joy (<reference osisRef="Acts.8.8">Ac 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.52">13:52</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.24">20:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.17">Ro 14:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.5.22">Ga 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.1.4">Php 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1Pe 1:8</reference>). Especially the godly shall rejoice at their final deliverance at Christ's second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.61.10">Is 61:10</reference>). <div eID="gen25100" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bf4fb184aa127a5adf407be6d055159d34f9150: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13265"/><div sID="gen25101" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13265"/>3. Solving the difficulty (Mal 3:15) that the wicked often now prosper. Their prosperity and the adversity of the godly shall soon be reversed. Yea, the righteous shall be the army attending Christ in His final destruction of the ungodly (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.43">2Sa 22:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.14">Psa 49:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.47.3">47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.7.10">Mi 7:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.5">Zec 10:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.2">1Co 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26">Re 2:26</reference>, 27; 19:14, 15).<div eID="gen25101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ashes--</hi>after having been burnt with the fire of judgment (Mal 4:1). <div eID="gen25102" type="x-p"/>
entries.9ab7548b969bd386dc1e866346c51c2d29b2d4ed: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13266"/><div sID="gen25103" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13266"/><hi type="bold">4. Remember ... law--</hi>"The law and all the prophets" were to be in force until John (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.13">Mt 11:13</reference>), no prophet intervening after Malachi; therefore they are told, "Remember the law," for in the absence of living prophets, they were likely to forget it. The office of Christ's forerunner was to bring them back to the law, which they had too much forgotten, and so "to make ready a people prepared for the Lord" at His coming (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>). God withheld prophets for a time that men might seek after Christ with the greater desire [Calvin]. The history of human advancement is marked by periods of rest, and again progress. So in Revelation: it is given for a time; then during its suspension men live on the memories of the past. After Malachi there was a silence of four hundred years; then a harbinger of light in the wilderness, ushering in the brightest of all the lights that had been manifested, but short-lived; then eighteen centuries during which we have been guided by the light which shone in that last manifestation. The silence has been longer than before, and will be succeeded by a more glorious and awful revelation than ever. John the Baptist was to "restore" the defaced image of "the law," so that the original might be recognized when it appeared among men [Hinds]. Just as "Moses" and "Elias" are here connected with the Lord's coming, so at the transfiguration they converse with Him, implying that the law and prophets which had prepared His way were now fulfilled in Him.<div eID="gen25103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25104" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">statutes ... judgments--</hi>ceremonial "statutes": "judgments" in civil questions at issue. "The law" refers to morals and religion. <div eID="gen25104" type="x-p"/>
entries.12c3bf6e578a71dcef1b8ae9dcde14e0f8194dbe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13267"/><div sID="gen25105" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13267"/><hi type="bold">5. I send you Elijah--</hi>as a means towards your "remembering the law" (Mal 4:4).<div eID="gen25105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25106" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the prophet--</hi>emphatical; not "the Tishbite"; for it is in his official, not his personal capacity, that his coming is here predicted. In this sense, John the Baptist was an Elijah in spirit (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.16">Lu 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference>), but not the literal Elijah; whence when asked, "Art thou Elias?" (<reference osisRef="John.1.21">Joh 1:21</reference>), He answered, "I am not." "Art thou that prophet?" "No." This implies that John, though knowing from the angel's announcement to his father that he was referred to by Mal 4:5 (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.17">Lu 1:17</reference>), whence he wore the costume of Elijah, yet knew by inspiration that he did not exhaustively fulfil all that is included in this prophecy: that there is a further fulfilment (compare Note, see on Mal 3:1). As Moses in Mal 4:4 represents the law, so Elijah represents the prophets. The Jews always understood it of the literal Elijah. Their saying is, "Messiah must be anointed by Elijah." As there is another consummating advent of Messiah Himself, so also of His forerunner Elijah; perhaps in person, as at the transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.3">Mt 17:3</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">Mt 17:11</reference>). He in his appearance at the transfiguration in that body on which death had never passed is the forerunner of the saints who shall be found alive at the Lord's second coming. <reference osisRef="Rev.11.3">Re 11:3</reference> may refer to the same witnesses as at the transfiguration, Moses and Elijah; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.6">Re 11:6</reference> identifies the latter (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.1">1Ki 17:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.17">Jas 5:17</reference>). Even after the transfiguration Jesus (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.11">Mt 17:11</reference>) speaks of Elijah's coming "to restore all things" as still future, though He adds that Elijah (in the person of John the Baptist) is come already in a sense (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.3.21">Ac 3:21</reference>). However, the future forerunner of Messiah at His second coming may be a prophet or number of prophets clothed with Elijah's power, who, with zealous upholders of "the law" clothed in the spirit of "Moses," may be the forerunning witnesses alluded to here and in <reference osisRef="Rev.11.2-Rev.11.12">Re 11:2-12</reference>. The words "before the ... dreadful day of the Lord," show that John cannot be exclusively meant; for he came before the day of Christ's coming in grace, not before His coming in terror, of which last the destruction of Jerusalem was the earnest (Mal 4:1; <reference osisRef="Joel.2.31">Joe 2:31</reference>). <div eID="gen25106" type="x-p"/>
entries.b4a5df938e9cfac8937edb69544ebf57022283ac: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13268"/><div sID="gen25107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13268"/><hi type="bold">6. turn ... heart of ... fathers to ... children, &c.--</hi>Explained by some, that John's preaching should restore harmony in families. But <reference osisRef="Luke.1.16">Lu 1:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.17">17</reference> substitutes for "the heart of the children to the fathers," "the disobedient to the wisdom of the just," implying that the reconciliation to be effected was that between the unbelieving disobedient children and the believing ancestors, Jacob, Levi, "Moses," and "Elijah" (just mentioned) (compare Mal 1:<reference osisRef="2Cor.2.4">2; 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.3">3:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.4">4</reference>). The threat here is that, if this restoration were not effected, Messiah's coming would prove "a curse" to the "earth," not a blessing. It proved so to guilty Jerusalem and the "earth," that is, the land of Judea when it rejected Messiah at His first advent, though He brought blessings (<reference osisRef="Gen.12.3">Ge 12:3</reference>) to those who accepted Him (<reference osisRef="John.1.11-John.1.13">Joh 1:11-13</reference>). Many were delivered from the common destruction of the nation through John's preaching (<reference osisRef="Rom.9.29">Ro 9:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.5">11:5</reference>). It will prove so to the disobedient at His second advent, though He comes to be glorified in His saints (<reference osisRef="2Thess.1.6-2Thess.1.10">2Th 1:6-10</reference>).<div eID="gen25107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25108" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">curse--</hi>Hebrew, Cherem, "a ban"; the fearful term applied by the Jews to the extermination of the guilty Canaanites. Under this ban Judea has long lain. Similar is the awful curse on all of Gentile churches who love not the Lord Jesus now (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.22">1Co 16:22</reference>). For if God spare not the natural branches, the Jews, much less will He spare unbelieving professors of the Gentiles (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.20">Ro 11:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.21">21</reference>). It is deeply suggestive that the last utterance from heaven for four hundred years before Messiah was the awful word "curse." Messiah's first word on the mount was "Blessed" (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.3">Mt 5:3</reference>). The law speaks wrath; the Gospel, blessing. Judea is now under the "curse" because it rejects Messiah; when the spirit of Elijah, or a literal Elijah, shall bring the Jewish children back to the Hope of their "fathers," blessing shall be theirs, whereas the apostate "earth" shall be "smitten with the curse" previous to the coming restoration of all things (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.13">Zec 12:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.12.14">14</reference>).<div eID="gen25108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen25109" type="x-p"/> May the writer of this Commentary and his readers have grace "to take heed to the sure word of prophecy as unto a light shining in a dark place, until the day dawn!" To the triune Jehovah be all glory ascribed for ever! The New Testament  <chapter eID="Mal.4"/><div eID="gen25109" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen24951" osisID="Mal" type="book"/>

entries.d4cf919a86155a9005a389818dbafb0eeb4731e3: <div eID="gen35941" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen35942" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35943" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35943" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen35942" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen35944" type="x-p"/> God's awful judgments on the wicked, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.1">Mal 4:1</reference>. Great blessedness of the righteous, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.2">Mal 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.3">Mal 4:3</reference>. The prophet then, with a solemnity becoming the last of the prophets, closes the Sacred Canon with enjoining the strict observance of the law till the forerunner already promised should appear, in the spirit of Elijah, to introduce the Messiah, and begin a new and everlasting dispensation, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.4-Mal.4.6">Mal 4:4-6</reference>. <div eID="gen35944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35945" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen35945" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35946" type="x-p"/> Behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven - The destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans. <div eID="gen35946" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35947" type="x-p"/> And all the proud - This is in reference to <reference osisRef="Mal.3.15">Mal 3:15</reference> of the preceding chapter. <div eID="gen35947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35948" type="x-p"/> The day that cometh shall burn them up - Either by famine, by sword, or by captivity. All those rebels shall be destroyed. <div eID="gen35948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35949" type="x-p"/> It shall leave them neither root nor branch - A proverbial expression for total destruction. Neither man nor child shall escape.
entries.80ee226a7a2d1531b83c1bc15611c34f002ffb4e: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen35949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35950" type="x-p"/> You that fear my name - The persons mentioned in the sixteenth verse of the preceding chapter, ye that look for redemption through the Messiah. <div eID="gen35950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35951" type="x-p"/> The Sun of righteousness - The Lord Jesus, the promised Messiah; the Hope of Israel. <div eID="gen35951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35952" type="x-p"/> With healing in his wings - As the sun, by the rays of light and heat, revives, cheers, and fructifies the whole creation, giving, through God, light and life everywhere; so Jesus Christ, by the influences of his grace and Spirit, shall quicken, awaken, enlighten, warm, invigorate heal, purify, and refine every soul that believes in him, and, by his wings or rays, diffuse these blessings from one end of heaven to another; everywhere invigorating the seeds of righteousness, and withering and drying up the seeds of sin. The rays of this Sun are the truths of his Gospel, and the influences of his Spirit. And at present these are universally diffused. <div eID="gen35952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35953" type="x-p"/> And ye shall go forth - Ye who believe on his name shall go forth out of Jerusalem when the Romans shall come up against it. After Cestius Gallus had blockaded the city for some days, he suddenly raised the siege. The Christians who were then in it, knowing, by seeing Jerusalem encompassed with armies, that the day of its destruction was come, when their Lord commanded them to flee into the mountains, took this opportunity to escape from Jerusalem, and go to Pella, in Coelesyria; so that no Christian life fell in the siege and destruction of this city. <div eID="gen35953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35954" type="x-p"/> But these words are of more general application and meaning; "ye shall go forth" in all the occupations of life, but particularly in the means of grace; and: - <div eID="gen35954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35955" type="x-p"/> Grow up as calves of the stall - Full of health, of life, and spirits; satisfied and happy.
entries.6b8d75a7a7d861690e0c94d393b44fe841f7babf: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen35955" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35956" type="x-p"/> Ye shall tread down - This may be the commission given to the Romans: Tread down the wicked people, tread down the wicked place; set it on fire, and let the ashes be trodden down under your feet.
entries.b19e2371256b8cc72fcda92e51fe9874911127b2: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen35956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35957" type="x-p"/> Remember ye the law of Moses - Where all these things are predicted. The Septuagint, Arabic, and Coptic, place this verse the last.
entries.97c53a61717082b21edb71424b50d87beb19b31a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen35957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35958" type="x-p"/> Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet - This is meant alone of John the Baptist, as we learn from <reference osisRef="Luk.1.17">Luk 1:17</reference> (note), in whose spirit and power he came.
entries.0ca1df506676ef2cc9dad6c412efc6672973f891: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen35958" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35959" type="x-p"/> And he shall turn (convert) the heart of the fathers (על al, with) the children - Or, together with the children; both old and young. Lest I come, and, finding them unconverted, smote the land with a curse, חרם cherem, utter extinction. So we find that, had the Jews turned to God, and received the Messiah at the preaching of John the Baptist and that of Christ and his apostles, the awful חרם cherem of final excision and execration would not have been executed upon them. However, they filled up the cup of their iniquity, and were reprobated, and the Gentiles elected in their stead. Thus, the last was first, and the first was last. Glory to God for his unspeakable gift! <div eID="gen35959" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35960" type="x-p"/> There are three remarkable predictions in this chapter: - <div eID="gen35960" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35961" type="x-p"/> 1. The advent of John Baptist, in the spirit and authority of Elijah. <div eID="gen35961" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35962" type="x-p"/> 2. The manifestation of Christ in the flesh, under the emblem of the Sun of righteousness. <div eID="gen35962" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35963" type="x-p"/> 3. The final destruction of Jerusalem, represented under the emblem of a burning oven, consuming every thing cast into it. <div eID="gen35963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35964" type="x-p"/> These three prophecies, relating to the most important facts that have ever taken place in the history of the world, announced here nearly four hundred years before their occurrence, have been most circumstantially fulfilled. <div eID="gen35964" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35965" type="x-p"/> In most of the Masoretic Bibles the fifth verse is repeated after the sixth - "Behold, I send unto you Elijah the prophet, before the great and terrible day of Jehovah come;" for the Jews do not like to let their sacred book end with a curse; and hence, in reading, they immediately subjoin the above verse, or else the fourth - "Remembering ye the law of Moses my servant." <div eID="gen35965" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35966" type="x-p"/> In one of my oldest MSS. the fifth verse is repeated, and written at full length: "Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet, before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord." In another, only these words are added: "Behold, I will send you Elijah." It is on this ground that the Jews expect the reappearance of Elijah the prophet, and at their marriage-feast always set a chair and knife and fork for this prophet, whom they suppose to be invisibly present. But we have already seen that John the Baptist, the forerunner of our Lord, was the person designed; for he came in the spirit and power of Elijah, (see on <reference osisRef="Mal.3.1">Mal 3:1</reference> (note)), and has fulfilled this prophetic promise. John is come, and the Lord Jesus has come also; he has shed his blood for the salvation of a lost world; he has ascended on high; he has sent forth his Holy Spirit; he has commissioned his ministers to proclaim to all mankind redemption in his blood; and he is ever present with them, and is filling the earth with righteousness and true holiness. Hallelujah! The kingdoms of this world are about to become the kingdoms of God and our Lord Jesus! And now, having just arrived at the end of my race in this work, and seeing the wonderful extension of the work of God in the earth, my heart prays: - O Jesus, ride on, till all are subdued, Thy mercy make known, and sprinkle thy blood; Display thy salvation, and teach the new song, To every nation, and people, and tongue! <div eID="gen35966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35967" type="x-p"/> In most MSS. and printed Masoretic Bibles there are only three chapters in this prophet, the fourth being joined to the third, making it twenty-four verses. <div eID="gen35967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen35968" type="x-p"/> In the Jewish reckonings the Twelve Minor Prophets make but one book; hence there is no Masoretic note found at the end of any of the preceding prophets, with accounts of its verses, sections etc.; but, at the end of Malachi we find the following table, which, though it gives the number of verses in each prophet, yet gives the total sum, middle verse, and sections, at the end of Malachi, thereby showing that they consider the whole twelve as constituting but one book.  <chapter eID="Mal.4"/> <div eID="gen35968" type="x-p"/> <div canonical="true" eID="gen35830" osisID="Mal" type="book"/>

entries.2c0da99397abe7373068b65ae63ab43e2339dd97: Mal 4:1-3 <div eID="gen16973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> This admonition to the ungodly is explained in Mal 4:1. by a picture of the separation which will be effected by the day of judgment. Mal 4:1. <hi type="italic">“For behold the day cometh burning like a furnace, and all the proud and every doer of wickedness become stubble, and the coming day will burn them, saith Jehovah of hosts, so that it will not leave them root or branch.</hi> Mal 4:2. <hi type="italic">But to you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness will rise and healing in its wings, and ye will go out and skip like stalled calves,</hi> Mal 4:3. <hi type="italic">And will tread down the ungodly, for they will be ashes under the soles of your feet in the day that I create, saith Jehovah of hosts.” </hi> The day of judgment will be to the ungodly like a burning furnace. “A fire burns more fiercely in a furnace than in the open air” (Hengstenberg). The ungodly will then resemble the stubble which the fire consumes (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.5.24">Isa 5:24</reference>; Zep 1:18; Oba 1:18, etc.). זדים and עשׂה רשׁעה point back to Mal 3:15. Those who are called blessed by the murmuring nation will be consumed by the fire, as stubble is burned up, and indeed <hi type="italic">all</hi> who do wickedness, and therefore the murmurers themselves. אשׁר before לא יעזב is a conjunction, <hi type="italic">quod</hi>; and the subject is not Jehovah, but the coming day. The figure “root and branch” is borrowed from a tree - the tree is the ungodly mass of the people (cf. <reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Amo 2:9</reference>) - and denotes total destruction, so that nothing will be left of them. To the righteous, on the other hand, the sun of righteousness will arise. <hi type="italic">Tsedâqâh</hi> is an epexegetical genitive of apposition. By the sun of righteousness the fathers, from Justin downwards, and nearly all the earlier commentators understand <hi type="italic">Christ</hi>, who is supposed to be described as the rising sun, like Jehovah in <reference osisRef="Ps.84.12">Psa 84:12</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.60.19">Isa 60:19</reference>; and this view is founded upon a truth, viz., that the coming of Christ brings justice and salvation. But in the verse before us the context does not sustain the personal view, but simply the idea that righteousness itself is regarded as a sun. <hi type="italic">Tsedâqâh</hi>, again, is not justification or the forgiveness of sins, as Luther and others suppose, for there will be no forgiving of sins on the day of judgment, but God will then give to every man reward or punishment according to his works. <hi type="italic">Tsedâqâh</hi> is here, what it frequently is in Isaiah (e.g., <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.46.13">Isa 46:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.5">Isa 51:5</reference>, etc.), righteousness in its consequences and effects, the sum and substance of salvation. Malachi uses <hi type="italic">tsedâqâh</hi>, righteousness, instead of ישׁע, salvation, with an allusion to the fact, that the ungodly complained of the absence of the judgment and righteousness of God, that is to say, the righteousness which not only punishes the ungodly, but also rewards the good with happiness and salvation. The sun of righteousness has מרפּא, healing, in its wings. The wings of the sun are the rays by which it is surrounded, and not a figure denoting swiftness. As the rays of the sun spread light and warmth over the earth for the growth and maturity of the plants and living creatures, so will the sun of righteousness bring the healing of all hurts and wounds which the power of darkness has inflicted upon the righteous. Then will they go forth, sc. from the holes and caves, into which they had withdrawn during the night of suffering and where they had kept themselves concealed, and skip like stalled calves (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.24">1Sa 28:24</reference>), which are driven from the stall to the pasture. On <hi type="italic">pūsh</hi>, see at Hab 1:8. And not only will those who fear God be liberated from all oppression, but they will also acquire power over the ungodly. They will tread down the wicked, who will then have become ashes, and lie like ashes upon the ground, having been completely destroyed by the fire of the judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Isa.26.5-Isa.26.6">Isa 26:5-6</reference>).
entries.17dfd34c4ee10a7b6f5beb8e9fa65e57959ab101: Mal 4:4-6 <div eID="gen16974" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> Concluding Admonition. - Mal 4:4. <hi type="italic">“Remember ye the law of Moses, my servant, which I commanded him upon Horeb for all Israel, statutes and rights.</hi><note placement="foot">The lxx have put Mal 4:4 at the end of the book, not to call attention to its great importance, but probably for the very same reason for which the <hi type="italic">Masora</hi> observes, at the close of our book, that in the יתקק, i.e., in the books of Isaiah, the twelve prophets, the Lamentations, and Ecclesiastes, the last verse but one of these books was to be repeated when they were read in the synagogue, namely, because the last verse had too harsh a sound. The transposition is unsuitable, inasmuch as the promise in Mal 4:5 and Mal 4:6 does not fit on to the idea expressed in Mal 4:2 and Mal 4:3, but only to that in Mal 4:4. According to the <hi type="italic">Masora</hi>, the ז in זכרוּ should be written as <hi type="italic">litera majusc.</hi>, although in many codd. it has the usual form; and this also is not to show the great importance of the verse, since these Masoretic indications have generally a different meaning, but in all probability it is simply to indicate that this is the only passage in the book of the twelve prophets in which the word is pronounced זכרוּ (cf. זכרו in Hos 12:6; Hos 14:8), whereas in the other books, with the exception of <reference osisRef="Job.18.17">Job 18:17</reference>, this is the only pronunciation that is met with.</note> <div eID="gen16975" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> Mal 4:5. <hi type="italic">Behold, I send you Elijah the prophet before the day of Jehovah comes, the great and terrible one.</hi> Mal 4:6. <hi type="italic">And he will turn the heart of the fathers to the sons, and the heart of the sons to their fathers, that I may not come and smite the land with the curse” </hi>(<hi type="italic">mit dem Banne</hi>, with the ban). The admonition, “Remember ye the law of Moses,” forms the conclusion not only of the last section (Malachi 3:13-4:3), but of the whole of the book of Malachi, and cannot be connected with Mal 4:3 in the sense of “Remember what Moses has written in the law concerning Christ, or concerning the judgment,” as Theod. Mops. and others maintain; nor must it be restricted to the time previous to the coming of the Messiah by the interpolation of <hi type="italic">interim</hi> (v. Til and Mich.). It is rather a perfectly general admonition to lay to heart and observe the law. For this is referred to here, “not according to its casual and transient form, but according to its real essence as expressing the holiness of God, just as in Mat 5:17” (Hengstenberg). Malachi thus closes by showing to the people what it is their duty to do, if on the day of judgment they would escape the curse with which transgressors are threatened in the law, and participate in the salvation so generally desired, and promised to those who fear God. By the expression “my servant,” the law is traced back to God as its author. At the giving of the law, Moses as only the servant of Jehovah. אשׁר צוּיתי אותו is not to be rendered “whom (אשׁר אותו) I charged with statutes and rights to all Israel” (Ewald, Bunsen), for we do not expect any further explanation of the relation in which Moses stood to the law, but “which I commanded him upon (to) all Israel.” <hi type="italic">Tsivvâh</hi> is construed with a double accusative, and also with על governing the person to whom the command refers, as in Ezr 8:17; <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.8">2Sa 14:8</reference>; Est 4:5. The words <hi type="italic">chuqqı̄ı̄m ūmishpâtı̄m</hi> are an epexegetical definition belonging to אשׁר: “which I commanded as statutes and rights,” i.e., consisting of these; and they recall to mind <reference osisRef="Deut.4.1">Deu 4:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Deut.8.14">Deu 8:14</reference>, where Moses urges upon the people the observance of the law, and also mentions <hi type="italic">Horeb</hi> as the place where the law was given. The whole of the admonition forms an antithesis to the rebuke in Mal 4:4, that from the days of their fathers they went away from the ordinances of Jehovah. These they are to be mindful to observe, that the Lord when He comes may not smite the land with the ban. <div eID="gen16976" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> In order to avert this curse from Israel, the Lord would send the prophet Elijah before His coming, for the purpose of promoting a change of heart in the nation. The identity of the prophet Elijah with the messenger mentioned in Mal 4:1, whom the Lord would send before Him, is universally acknowledged. But there is a difference of opinion as to the question, who is the Elijah mentioned here? The notion was a very ancient one, and one very widely spread among the rabbins and fathers, that the prophet Elijah, who was caught up to heaven, would reappear (compare the history of the exposition of our verse in Hengstenberg’s <hi type="italic">Christology</hi>, vol. iv. p. 217 translation). The lxx thought of him, and rendered אליּה הנּביא by Ἠλίαν τὸν Θεσβίτην; so also did Sirach Sirach(48:10) and the Jews in the time of Christ (Joh 1:21; <reference osisRef="Matt.17.10">Mat 17:10</reference>); and so have Hitzig, Maurer, and Ewald in the most recent times. But this view is proved to be erroneous by such passages as Hos 3:5; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.24">Eze 37:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Jer.30.9">Jer 30:9</reference>, where the sending of David the king as the true shepherd of Israel is promised. Just as in these passages we cannot think of the return or resurrection of the David who had long been dead; but a king is meant who will reign over the nation of God in the mind and spirit of David; so the Elijah to be sent can only be a prophet with the spirit or power of Elijah the Tishbite. The second David was indeed to spring from the family of David, because to the seed of David there had been promised the eternal possession of the throne. The prophetic calling, on the other hand, was not hereditary in the prophet’s house, but rested solely upon divine choice and endowment with the Spirit of God; and consequently by Elijah we are not to understand a lineal descendant of the Tishbite, but simply a prophet in whom the spirit and power of Elijah are revived, as Ephr. Syr., Luther, Calvin, and most of the Protestant commentators have maintained. But the reason why this prophet Elijah is named is to be sought for, not merely in the fact that Elijah was called to his work as a reformer in Israel at a period which was destitute of faith and of the true fear of Jehovah, and which immediately preceded a terrible judgment (Koehler), but also and more especially in the power and energy with which Elijah rose up to lead back the ungodly generation of his own time to the God of the fathers. The one does not exclude but rather includes the other. The greater the apostasy, the greater must be the power which is to stem it, so as to rescue those who suffer themselves to be rescued, before the judgment bursts over such as are hardened. For <hi type="italic">Mal 4:5</hi>, compare Joe 3:4. This Elijah, according to Mal 4:6, is to lead back the heart of the fathers to the sons, and the heart of the sons to their fathers. The meaning of this is not that he will settle disputes in families, or restore peace between parents and children; for the leading sin of the nation at the time of our prophet was not family quarrels, but estrangement from God. The fathers are rather the ancestors of the Israelitish nation, the patriarchs, and generally the pious forefathers, such as David and the godly men of his time. The sons or children are the degenerate descendants of Malachi’s own time and the succeeding ages. “The hearts of the godly fathers and the ungodly sons are estranged from one another. The bond of union, viz., common love to God, is wanting. The fathers are ashamed of their children, the children of their fathers” (Hengstenberg). This chasm between them Elijah is to fill up. Turning the heart of the fathers to the sons does not mean merely directing the love of the fathers to the sons once more, but also restoring the heart of the fathers, in the sons, or giving to the sons the fathers’ disposition and affections. Then will the heart of the sons also return to their fathers, turn itself towards them, so that they will be like-minded with the pious fathers. Elijah will thereby prepare the way of the Lord to His people, that at His coming He may not smite the land with the ban. The ban involves extermination. Whoever and whatever was laid under the ban was destroyed (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.27.28-Lev.27.29">Lev 27:28-29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.13.16-Deut.13.17">Deu 13:16-17</reference>; and my <hi type="italic">Bibl. Archäol.</hi> i. §70). This threat recals to mind the fate of the Canaanites who were smitten with the ban (<reference osisRef="Deut.20.17-Deut.20.18">Deu 20:17-18</reference>). If Israel resembles the Canaanites in character, it will also necessarily share the fate of that people (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.12.29">Deu 12:29</reference>). <div eID="gen16977" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> The New Testament gives us a sufficient explanation of the historical allusion or fulfilment of our prophecy. The prophet Elijah, whom the Lord would send before His own coming, was sent in the person of John the Baptist. Even before his birth he was announced to his father by the angel Gabriel as the promised Elijah, by the declaration that he would turn many of the children of Israel to the Lord their God, and go before Him in the spirit and power of Elijah to turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the unbelieving to the wisdom of the just (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.16-Luke.1.17">Luk 1:16-17</reference>). This address of the angel gives at the same time an authentic explanation of Mal 4:5 and Mal 4:6 of our prophecy: the words “and the heart of the children to their fathers” being omitted, as implied in the turning of the heart of the fathers to the sons, and the explanatory words “and the unbelieving to the wisdom of the just” being introduced in their place; and the whole of the work of John, who was to go before the Lord in the spirit and power of Elijah, being described as “making ready a prepared people for the Lord.” The appearance and ministry of John the Baptist answered to this announcement of the angel, and is so described in <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1-Matt.3.12">Mat 3:1-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.1.2-Mark.1.8">Mar 1:2-8</reference>; Luke 3:2-18, that the allusion to our prophecy and the original passage (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Isa 40:3</reference>) is obvious at once. Even by his outward appearance and his dress John announced himself as the promised prophet Elijah, who by the preaching of repentance and baptism was preparing the way for the Lord, who would come after him with the winnowing shovel to winnow His floor, and gather the wheat into His granary, but who would burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire. Christ Himself also not only assured the people (in Mat 11:10., Luk 7:27.) that John was the messenger announced by Malachi and the Elijah who was to come, but also told His disciples (Mat 17:1.; Mar 9:1.) that Elijah, who was to come first and restore all things, had already come, though the people had not acknowledged him. And even Joh 1:21 is not at variance with these statements. When the messengers of the Sanhedrim came to John the Baptist to ask whether he was Elias, and he answered, “I am not,” he simply gave a negative reply to their question, interpreted in the sense of a personal reappearance of Elijah the Tishbite, which was the sense in which they meant it, but he also declared himself to be the promised forerunner of the Lord by applying to his own labours the prophecy contained in Isa 40:3. <div eID="gen16978" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16979" type="x-p"/> And as the prophet Elijah predicted by Malachi appeared in John the Baptist, so did the Lord come to His temple in the appearing of Jesus Christ. The opinion, which was very widely spread among the fathers and Catholic commentators, and which has also been adopted by many of the more modern Protestant theologians (e.g., Menken and H. Olshausen), viz., that our prophecy was only provisionally fulfilled in the coming of John the Baptist and the incarnation of the Son of God in Jesus Christ, and that its true fulfilment will only take place at the second coming of Christ to judge the world, in the actual appearance of the risen Elijah by which it will be preceded, is not only at variance with the statements of the Lord concerning John the Baptist, which have been already quoted, but as no tenable foundation in our prophecy itself. The prophets of the Old Testament throughout make no allusion to any second coming of the Lord to His people. The day of the Lord, which they announce as the day of judgment, commenced with the appearance on earth of Christ, the incarnate Logos; and Christ Himself declared that He had come into the world for judgment (Joh 9:39, cf. Joh 3:19 and Joh 12:40), viz., for the judgment of separating the believing from the ungodly, to give eternal life to those who believe on His name, and to bring death and condemnation to unbelievers. This judgment burst upon the Jewish nation not long after the ascension of Christ. Israel rejected its Saviour, and was smitten with the ban at the destruction of Jerusalem in the Roman war; and both people and land lie under this ban to the present day.
